statement.p:
In this activity, we will look at linear combinations of a pair of vectors,
\vvec = \left[\begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]
and
\wvec = \left[\begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right] .

interactive.shortdescription: An interactive diagram to study linear combinations.

description.p: In the background of this interactive diagram is a coordinate grid and a set of labelled axes. There are also two vectors \vvec and \wvec shown, both starting at the origin. There is also a set of lines, each of which is parallel to \vvec, passing through integer multiples of \wvec. In the same way, there is a second set of lines, each of which is parallel to \wvec, passing through integer multiples of \vvec. These two sets of parallel lines form a skewed coordinate grid.

Across the top of the diagram are two sliders, which can be used to vary two parameters labelled c and d. When one of those parameters is varied, the vector c\vvec+d\wvec shown moving parallel to one of the sets of skewed grid lines.

sidebyside.p: There is an interactive diagram, available at , that accompanies this activity.

instructions.p:
The diagram below can be used to construct linear combinations whose weights c and d may be varied using the sliders at the top. The vectors \vvec and \wvec are outlined while the linear combination
c\vvec + d\wvec
is shaded red.

li.p: The weight d is initially set to 0. Explain what happens as you vary c while keeping d=0. How is this related to scalar multiplication?
What is the linear combination of \vvec and \wvec when c = 1 and d=-2? You may find this result using the diagram, but you should also verify it by computing the linear combination.
Describe the vectors that arise when the weight d is set to 1 and c is varied. How is this related to our investigations in the preview activity?
Can the vector \left[\begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 0 \end{array} \right] be expressed as a linear combination of \vvec and \wvec? If so, what are the weights c and d?
Can the vector \left[\begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 0 \end{array} \right] be expressed as a linear combination of \vvec and \wvec? If so, what are the weights c and d?
Verify the result from the previous part by algebraically finding the weights c and d that form the linear combination \left[\begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 0 \end{array} \right].

Can the vector \left[\begin{array}{r} 1.3 \\ -1.7 \end{array} \right] be expressed as a linear combination of \vvec and \wvec? What about the vector \left[\begin{array}{r} 15.2 \\ 7.1 \end{array} \right]?
Are there any two-dimensional vectors that cannot be expressed as linear combinations of \vvec and \wvec?
When we vary c with d=0, the linear combination moves along the line defined by \vvec.
When d=1 and c is allowed to vary, the linear combinations lie on the line through \wvec parallel to \vvec.
If the weights c=0 and d=0, then the linear combination is the vector \twovec{0}{0}.
If the weights c=2 and d=-1, then the linear combination is the vector \twovec{3}{0}.

Every two-dimensional vector can be written as a linear combination of \vvec and \wvec because the coefficient matrix of the linear system remains the same. Since that coefficient matrix has a pivot position in every row, the augmented matrix can never have a pivot position in the rightmost column.
The linear combinations lie on the line defined by \vvec.
\twovec{0}{-3}.
They lie on the line through \wvec parallel to \vvec.
Yes, with weights c=d=0.
Yes, with weights c=2 and d=-1.
This can be done by writing the appropriate linear system for the weights.
No, any two-dimensional vector can be expressed as a linear combination of \vvec and \wvec.
